'''Andre Franke''', born on 16 October 1978, is a [[geneticist]], academic, and university professor. He is a Full W3 Professor of [[Molecular Medicine]] at the [[Kiel University|Christian-Albrechts-University of Kiel]], and a managing director at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.metaorganism-research.com/researchers/prof-dr-andre-franke/|title=Prof. Dr. Andre Franke - Origin and Function of Metaorganisms}}</ref>

Franke is most known for his work on genetics, [[Genome-wide association study|genome-wide association studies]], [[microbiome]], and [[internal medicine]] research. He integrates [[bioinformatics]] developments with novel technologies, chronic inflammatory diseases, and has studied the [[genetic architecture]] of different complex diseases and traits.<ref name=poi>{{cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Andre-Franke-3|title=Andre Franke - Research Gate Profile}}</ref>

==Education==
Franke enrolled at the Christian-Albrecht University of Kiel and graduated with a Diploma in Biology in 2003.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ikmb.uni-kiel.de/people/scientists/andre-franke|title=University of Kiel Profile}}</ref> From 2004 until 2006, he undertook research in complex disease genetics for a [[Dr. rer. nat.|''Doctor rerum naturalium'']] at the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology under the supervision of [[Stefan Schreiber]] and [[Thomas C.G. Bosch]]. His dissertation was titled "A systematic genome-wide association analysis for Inflammatory Bowel Diseases."<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.ikmb.uni-kiel.de/sites/default/files/pdfs/dissertations/Franke2006-%20Inflammatory%20Bowel%20diseases%20(1).pdf|title= A systematic genome-wide association analysis for the Inflammatory Bowel Diseases }}</ref>

==Career==
Following his ''doctor rerum naturalium'' degree and a short postdoc, Franke started his academic career as an [[assistant professor]] for ''Epithelial Barrier Diseases'' funded by the DFG Cluster of Excellence 306 between 2008 and 2011.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ous-research.no/nopsc/docs/NoPSC_Ann_report2010_lowres.pdf|title= Annual report 2010 - Norwegian PSC Research Center}}</ref>

While mentored by Richard S. Blumberg, Franke also served as a guest scientist at the [[Eli and Edythe L. Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard|Broad Institute]] of MIT and Harvard in Boston in 2011.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-03177-5|title=Author Correction: Evaluating drug targets through human loss-of-function genetic variation}}</ref> He was promoted to a full W3 professorship and has been holding this appointment since 2016.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mitarget.org/people/prof-dr-rer-nat-andre-franke/|title=Facts - Prof. Dr. rer. nat. Andre Franke - Mitarget}}</ref>

Since 2011, Franke has been the Director of the Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://medicalxpress.com/news/2020-09-neanderthal-genes-liability-covid-patients.html|title=Study: Neanderthal genes are a liability for COVID patients}}</ref>

==Research==
Franke has authored over 730 publications, and has a [[Web of Science|Web of science]] h-index of 110.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.webofscience.com/wos/author/record/901474|title= Franke, Andre –Web of Science Profile}}</ref> His research focus includes genetics/genomics/immunogenetics, bioinformatics, the human microbiome, and high-throughput sequencing technologies. He has worked on genome-wide association studies, [[single-nucleotide polymorphism]]-based analyses, and complex diseases. He has explored the aspects of genetic architecture, genetic variability, and population genetics whereas his main disease focus has been inflammatory bowel diseases, including [[Crohn's disease]] and ulcerative colitis. Other research foci have been the diseases psoriasis and primary sclerosing cholangitis.<ref name=poi/><ref name=qwer>{{cite web|url=https://www.dwih-newyork.org/files/2018/11/GCRI-Interview-Franke.pdf|title=GCRI INTERVIEW}}</ref>

===Genome wide association study===
Franke's work in genome wide association studies mainly focused on the identification of susceptibility genes in inflammatory diseases such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. During his PhD in 2006, he performed the first genome-wide association scan of nonsynonymous SNPs in a case-control panel with Crohn's disease patients and control individuals. The identification of a Crohn's-associated coding SNP in the ATG16L1 led to the description that autophagy is an important pathway that is impaired in patients with Crohn's disease.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nature.com/articles/ng1954 |title= A genome-wide association scan of nonsynonymous SNPs identifies a susceptibility variant for Crohn's disease in ATG16L1}}</ref> A 2010 research study which undertook the genome-wide association meta-analysis and replication study for Crohn's disease identified 71 novel loci that are associated with the disease, further completing the genetic architecture of inflammatory bowel diseases.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nature.com/articles/ng.717|title= Genome-wide meta-analysis increases to 71 the number of confirmed Crohn's disease susceptibility loci}}</ref> Later on, Franke joined the International IBD Genetics Consortium (IIBDGC) where he is on the Management Committee.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ibdgenetics.org/|title= About - A global network of IBD consortia}}</ref>

Franke conducted systematic trans-ethnic association studies for IBD including people of European, East Asian, Indian, and Iranian descent. Besides performing traditional genome-wide association analyses,<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nature.com/articles/ng.3359|title= Association analyses identify 38 susceptibility loci for inflammatory bowel disease and highlight shared genetic risk across populations}}</ref> he also systematically investigated the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region in IBD cohorts of different ethnicities.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Transethnic analysis of the human leukocyte antigen region for ulcerative colitis reveals not only shared but also ethnicity-specific disease associations |year=2021 |pmid=33555323 |last1=Degenhardt |first1=F. |last2=Mayr |first2=G. |last3=Wendorff |first3=M. |last4=Boucher |first4=G. |last5=Ellinghaus |first5=E. |last6=Ellinghaus |first6=D. |last7=Elabd |first7=H. |last8=Rosati |first8=E. |last9=Hübenthal |first9=M. |last10=Juzenas |first10=S. |last11=Abedian |first11=S. |last12=Vahedi |first12=H. |last13=Thelma |first13=B. Franke has also investigated the genetics of psoriasis. He performed several genetic association studies for this disease.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/ng.311|title= Genome-wide scan reveals association of psoriasis with IL-23 and NF-κB pathways}}</ref> 
Additional research centered on risk assessment of psoriatic arthritis development in psoriasis patients, highlighting that underlying genetic differences between psoriasis subtypes can be used for individualized subtype risk assessments.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-06672-6|title= Genetic signature to provide robust risk assessment of psoriatic arthritis development in psoriasis patients}}</ref> He also contributed to a study that aimed to identify genetic variants for gallstone disease. Through transcript mapping, mutation detection, and association analysis in an ethnically different population, rs11887534 (ABCG8-D19H) was identified as a disease-relevant factor.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://aasldpubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/hep.26009|title= Genetic and functional identification of the likely causative variant for cholesterol gallstone disease at the ABCG5/8 lithogenic locus|year= 2013|doi= 10.1002/hep.26009|last1= von Kampen|first1= Oliver|last2= Buch|first2= Stephan|last3= Nothnagel|first3= Michael|last4= Azocar|first4= Lorena|last5= Molina|first5= Hector|last6= Brosch|first6= Mario|last7= Erhart|first7= Wiebke|last8= von Schönfels|first8= Witigo|last9= Egberts|first9= Jan|last10= Seeger|first10= Marcus|last11= Arlt|first11= Alexander|last12= Balschun|first12= Tobias|last13= Franke|first13= Andre|last14= Lerch|first14= Markus M.|last15= Mayerle|first15= Julia|last16= Kratzer|first16= Wolfgang|last17= Boehm|first17= Bernhard O.|last18= Huse|first18= Klaus|last19= Schniewind|first19= Bodo|last20= Tiemann|first20= Katharina|last21= Jiang|first21= Zhao-Yan|last22= Han|first22= Tian-Quan|last23= Mittal|first23= Balraj|last24= Srivastava|first24= Anshika|last25= Fenger|first25= Mogens|last26= Jørgensen|first26= Torben|last27= Schirin-Sokhan|first27= Ramin|last28= Tönjes|first28= Anke|last29= Wittenburg|first29= Henning|last30= Stumvoll|first30= Michael|journal= Hepatology|volume= 57|issue= 6|pages= 2407–2417|pmid= 22898925|s2cid= 1692664|display-authors= 1|url-access= subscription|hdl= 10533/237863|hdl-access= free}}</ref>

In 2020, during the first wave of the Corona virus epidemic, Franke investigated the genetic susceptibility to SARS-CoV-2 and also tried to identify genetic factors that contribute to the variation and development of COVID-19 such as disease severity.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/06/03/health/coronavirus-blood-type-genetics.html|title=Genes May Leave Some People More Vulnerable to Severe Covid-19 |website=[[The New York Times]] }}</ref> This first genome-wide association study for COVID-19 identified the ABO blood-group system as a factor for susceptibility for SARS-CoV-2 infection whereas variants in the gene cluster on chromosome 3p21.31 were determined as important factors for disease severity.<ref>{{cite journal|title= Genomewide Association Study of Severe Covid-19 with Respiratory Failure|journal= New England Journal of Medicine|year= 2020|volume= 383|issue= 16|pages= 1522–1534|doi= 10.1056/nejmoa2020283|pmid= 32558485|author1= Severe Covid-19 GWAS Group|last2= Ellinghaus|first2= D.|last3= Degenhardt|first3= F.|last4= Bujanda|first4= L.|last5= Buti|first5= M.|last6= Albillos|first6= A.|last7= Invernizzi|first7= P.|last8= Fernández|first8= J.|last9= Prati|first9= D.|last10= Baselli|first10= G.|last11= Asselta|first11= R.|last12= Grimsrud|first12= M. Franke further coordinated genetic studies that led to the identification of the first disease genes for chronic venous disease<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/srep45652|title=Genome-wide association analysis for chronic venous disease identifies EFEMP1 and KCNH8 as susceptibility loci}}</ref> and hemorrhoids disease (first 102 disease loci for this disease).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.uksh.de/Das+UKSH/Presse/Presseinformationen/2021/Umfangreiche+Gen_Studie+bringt+neue+Erkenntnisse+zu+den+Ursachen+von+%E2%80%9EH%C3%A4morrhoiden%E2%80%9C-p-187672.html|title= Extensive gene study brings new insights into the causes of "hemorrhoids"}}</ref>

===Microbiome studies===
Later in his career he focused on sequence analysis of the microbiome, which could at that point in time be analyzed using culture-free sequence-based analyses. In an interview with the German Centre for Research and Innovation – New York, he addressed that his current work aims to pinpoint "the relevant genes in the human genome that may be involved in host-microbiome interactions."<ref name=qwer/> Important scientific contributions were the first microbiome genome-wide association studies (mGWAS) that led to the identification of different genes and variants in the human genome that are involved in host-bacterial interaction.
